subject: Clarify: usage metrics & commit-tier language for hosted API

Cc: Tom Huang <tom.huang@acme.com>

Subject: Questions on commit tiers + streaming billing accuracy

Hi Karthik —

Thanks again for the demo last week. Procurement and Legal flagged a couple of areas we need more color on before we can move to redlines:

1) Billable tokens definition: we need explicit language describing whether billable tokens = input + output tokens, and how partial tokens or interim streaming chunks are rounded.
2) Streaming/batched responses: for our use case we stream long-form answers; we need to understand if streaming incurs any per-chunk rounding that could magnify billing compared to batch responses.
3) Commit tiers & true-up: how are monthly commits measured (calendar month vs rolling 30 days)? Is there automatic rollover, or a true-up at month end?

Can you send proposed contract snippets and a simple worked example (e.g., 1M tokens inbound, 3.7M outbound streamed over 14 streaming responses) so we can show Legal? I've attached our list of compliance questions.

Appreciate it — Samantha

Samantha Ortiz
Head of Platform Partnerships
Acme Corp

Hi Samantha —

Thanks — great list. Quick answers up front, and I attached a compact table that walks through a sample usage math and two draft clause options (conservative vs customer-favorable).

Summary:
- Billable tokens: by default we measure "billable tokens" as the sum of input (prompt) and output (response) tokens consumed by the request.
- Rounding: we round up to the nearest whole token per request. For streaming responses, billing is based on tokens emitted by the model; we do not add an extra per-chunk surcharge.
- Streaming granularity: runtime reports tokens as they're generated. To avoid excessive micro-billing, we aggregate emitted tokens at the request level and apply the per-request rounding.
- Commit measurement: commits are measured on a calendar-month basis by default, with a single monthly true-up on the first business day of the following month. We can scope to rolling 30 days if you need.

I'm attaching a worked example (usage-metrics-table.xlsx) and a draft SLA/metric clause (redwood-draft-sla-clauses.pdf). Ben and Marissa are cc'd — Ben, can you confirm the streaming aggregation logic in writing so Legal has the exact technical wording?

Next steps: if these items look OK, Marissa can pull together the simple clause to insert into the SOW and I can loop in Contracts for the commit language.

Best,

Hi all —

Following up with the technical detail Samantha asked for so Legal has precise language. Below is proposed wording and an illustrative example. Feel free to copy/paste into the contract draft.

Proposed contract snippet (technical wording):
"Billable Tokens" means the sum of tokens present in the request prompt (input tokens) and tokens produced by Redwood's models in response (output tokens). For the avoidance of doubt, Billable Tokens are measured per request. Tokens are integer counts; partial token values are rounded up to the nearest whole token at the time the request is completed. For streaming responses, tokens emitted by the model are accumulated for the request and charged according to the same per-request token count and rounding policy.

Streaming aggregation (clarifying note):
- Runtime emits tokens incrementally; Redwood aggregates emitted tokens per request and reports a single token count for billing when the request finishes or the connection closes. There is no additional per-chunk or per-emit rounding beyond the per-request rounding described above.

Example (worked):
- Single request: 1,243 input tokens; streaming response generates 37,812 tokens in 14 onMessage events. Billable tokens for the request = 1,243 + 37,812 = 39,055 tokens (rounded up per request).
- If a user aborts mid-stream after 10,000 tokens emitted, billable tokens = input + emitted tokens at abort time; rounded up to nearest token.

Commit tiers / measurement example:
- Calendar month commit = 100M tokens. Usage across the month is summed from each request's billable token totals. On the first business day following month end Redwood calculates actual usage and applies one of: (a) true-up invoice for overage, or (b) credit for under-consumption per the negotiated SOW.

Optional adjustments we can offer for enterprise deals: monthly smoothing (rolling 30-day average) or quarterly true-ups to reduce volatility.

Please let me know if Legal needs the snippet to reference exact header fields in logs (we can include log sample lines).

Ben Carter
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
ben.carter@redwood.com

Karthik / Ben —

Thanks for the quick write-up and examples. A few points from Legal:

1) We prefer explicit ceiling language where possible — e.g., maximum per-request rounding impact should be stated. The example math is helpful but we need a worst-case statement (e.g., rounding up a 0.9 token delta per request * large number of requests).
2) For long-running streams and aborted connections, Acme requests a 24-hour backstop: if the connection is lost due to network interruption and the client reconnects within 24 hours to resume the same logical conversation, we ask that Redwood use the combined emitted token count for billing rather than treating as two separate requests.
3) Commit true-up cadence: Acme would prefer quarterly smoothing rather than monthly true-ups for predictability.

Can you confirm whether Redwood can: (a) include a "rounding exposure" cap (for example, per-request rounding will not result in more than 0.5% additional billable tokens across a monthly aggregation), and (b) support a 24-hour stream-resume aggregation behavior as an enterprise configurable option? If yes, we can proceed with limited redlines.

—Acme Legal

Hi —

Thanks for the clear asks. I've discussed this with Product and Contracts; below are the compromise options Redwood can accept for an enterprise SOW:

1) Rounding exposure cap: Redwood can agree to a contractual cap on rounding exposure. Proposed language: "Redwood warrants that per-request rounding will not cause total billed tokens to exceed actual token counts by more than 0.6% in any given calendar month. If the rounding exposure exceeds 0.6% in a month, Redwood will issue a credit for the excess on the next invoice." This is measurable from our logs.

2) Stream-resume aggregation: Redwood can support a 24-hour resume window as an enterprise-configurable option. Proposed language: "For long-running sessions that are interrupted due to network conditions, if the client reconnects within 24 hours and presents the original session identifier, Redwood will aggregate emitted tokens from the interrupted and resumed sessions for billing purposes, treating them as a single logical request." Implementation notes: requires a session-id header documented in the SOW; engineering will enable a session resume flag at the tenancy level.

3) Commit cadence: Redwood can offer quarterly smoothing as a billing option: the customer's quarterly commit will be divided into monthly allocations for operational metering, and true-ups performed at quarter end (instead of monthly) to reduce volatility.

If that sounds workable I will have Contracts add the specific clause language into the SOW and share for Acme's review.

Karthik
